name: Lumecca IPL

lead: Lumecca is an InMode intense pulsed light device used in clinics for brown spots and facial redness. IPL uses broad-spectrum flashes rather than a single laser wavelength.
Studies naming Lumecca are few and small, mostly in vessel response and rosacea.

paras: Flashlamp light is absorbed by melanin or haemoglobin, heating pigment or small vessels, with surface cooling to protect skin.
IPL complications can include hyperpigmentation; photosensitising drugs and damaged skin are contraindications, and one manufacturer states IPL suits light to medium skin tones.

lead: Lumecca is a high-intensity intense pulsed light (IPL) device made by InMode, used in clinics for facial pigment and redness.[1] IPL is not a laser: a xenon flashlamp emits broad-spectrum, non-coherent light, and filters select which light-absorbing targets (melanin or haemoglobin) are heated.[2]

Published research naming Lumecca is limited to small studies. A study of 38 volunteers used three Lumecca IPL sessions and measured the response of dilated facial blood vessels with quantitative methods[1], and a 20-patient study assessed erythema reduction in rosacea after polychromatic light treatments.[3] A 2025 registered trial compares IPL, an anti-redness cosmetic and their combination in rosacea.[4]

paras: IPL devices use a flashlamp that emits roughly 400 to 1200 nm, with filters that cut off shorter and longer wavelengths. Melanin, haemoglobin and water absorb the light and heat, and cooling protects the skin surface.[2] IPL was invented by Shimon Eckhouse in 1992, with US clearances for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.[2]

Reference sources list photorejuvenation, pigmentation, sun damage, thread veins, rosacea, acne and melasma among IPL uses.[2] The Lumecca-specific study found that three treatments allowed vessel response to be quantified in 38 volunteers.[1] The rosacea study authors describe IPL as a recognised treatment for erythema and telangiectasia and emphasise combining clinical assessment with imaging analysis.[3]

Reference sources note that complications such as hyperpigmentation can occur, that photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are contraindications, and that one manufacturer advises IPL and laser devices only for light to medium skin tones.[2]

A 38-volunteer study used three Lumecca IPL treatments to evaluate quantitative methods for assessing dilated facial vessels.[1] A 20-patient study assessed rosacea erythema after polychromatic light treatments.[3] NCT07729540, a 60-participant trial started in 2025, compares IPL, an anti-redness dermocosmetic and both together in rosacea.[4] All are small, and results of the registered trial are not available in the registry entry cited here.

timeline.event: Shimon Eckhouse invents intense pulsed light.[2]
First US clearance for IPL on vascular lesions.[2]
US clearance for IPL hair removal.[2]
